prompt: Who has the last say on the order of the Product Backlog? Choose the best answer.

options.text: The Stakeholders.
The CEO.
The Developers.
The Scrum Master.
The Product Owner.

explanation: The Product Owner is accountable for effective Product Backlog management. This includes its content, availability, and ordering.
source: Scrum Guide 2020 — Product Backlog; Product Owner accountabilities.

prompt: Who is required to conform to the Definition of Done? Choose the best answer.

options.text: The QA department
The Product Owner
The Scrum Team
The Developers

explanation: The Developers are required to conform to the Definition of Done.
source: Scrum Guide 2020 — Definition of Done; Developers’ accountability.

prompt: True or False: It is important that the product increment is released to production or shipped to customers at the end of each Sprint.

options.text: True
False

explanation: The Increment must be usable, but Scrum does not require releasing at the end of every Sprint. The moment a Product Backlog item meets the Definition of Done, an Increment is born.
source: Scrum Guide 2020 — Increment (releasable at any time; DoD).

prompt: A Product Goal is… Choose the best two answers.

options.text: …placed in the Sprint Backlog.
…an optional artifact in Scrum.
…forbidden in Scrum.
…the long-term objective for the Scrum Team.
...in the Product Backlog.

explanation: The Product Goal is the long-term objective for the Scrum Team and lives in the Product Backlog.
source: Scrum Guide 2020 — Product Goal; Product Backlog.

prompt: While under development, the environment in which a product will be used changes and emerges. What is the effect on the Product Backlog? Choose the best answer

options.text: It is converted into a requirements specification to ensure stability.
It is archived and a new Product Backlog is created to take its place.
There is no effect, because it has to stay the same until the end of the project.
It evolves to reflect what the product needs to be most valuable.

explanation: The Product Backlog is a living, emergent artifact that evolves to maximize product value.
source: Scrum Guide 2020 — Product Backlog (emergent, dynamic).

prompt: Which of the following statements about the Product Backlog is NOT true? Choose the best answer.

options.text: The Product Backlog is dynamic.
The Product Backlog constantly changes to identify what the product needs to be.
The Product Backlog evolves as the product and the environment in which it will be used evolves.
The Product Backlog is complete when the final product Increment is considered Done.

explanation: A Product Backlog is never complete; it remains an emergent list as long as the product exists.
source: Scrum Guide 2020 — Product Backlog (emergent, never complete).

prompt: During a Sprint, when is new work or further decomposition of work added to the Sprint Backlog? Choose the best answer.

options.text: When the Scrum Master has time to enter them.
During the Daily Scrum after the Developers approve them.
When the Product Owner identifies a new work.
As soon as possible after they are identified.

explanation: The Sprint Backlog is updated throughout the Sprint as more is learned.
source: Scrum Guide 2020 — Sprint Backlog (emerges and is updated during the Sprint).

prompt: If quality assurance work does not occur as part of the development work within a Sprint, which benefits are lost? Choose all that apply.

options.text: The Product Backlog burndown is not transparent
The project manager cannot effectively update the plan
The next Sprint will probably be interrupted with bugs that are being found
The increment is probably not usable.

explanation: Without built-in quality, the Increment may not be usable and future Sprints risk interruption due to defects.
source: Scrum Guide 2020 — Increment; Definition of Done; built-in quality.

prompt: What are some consequences if a Scrum Team does not have a consistent Definition of Done from Sprint to Sprint? Choose the best answer.

options.text: The Product Owner may be unable to gauge the progress toward his/her goals.
The Developers may not know how many Product Backlog items they can complete in a Sprint
The Scrum Team and the stakeholders may not know what they are inspecting at the Sprint Review
The Developers may not know what work is entailed in completing selected.
All answers apply.

explanation: A shared Definition of Done ensures transparency of what 'done' means, enabling planning, inspection, and progress tracking.
source: Scrum Guide 2020 — Definition of Done (shared understanding, transparency).

prompt: Which statement best describes the Sprint Backlog as an outcome of the Sprint Planning? Choose the best answer.

options.text: Each task is estimated in hours.
It is a complete list of all work to be done in a Sprint.
Every item has a designated owner.
It is ordered by the Product Owner.
It is a plan by and for the Developers.

explanation: The Sprint Backlog is a plan by and for the Developers—a real-time picture of work to achieve the Sprint Goal.
source: Scrum Guide 2020 — Sprint Backlog (plan by and for the Developers).

prompt: After a Sprint Retrospective there are several high priority improvements identified by the Scrum Team. What would be the next course of action? Choose the best answer.

options.text: Add at least one high priority item into the Product Backlog.
Add the highest priority item into the Product Backlog.
Hand the list of high priority items over to the HR-Department and have them deal with them.
Aim for the highest priority item(s) to be addressed as soon as possible.

explanation: The most impactful improvements are addressed as soon as possible; they may even be added to the next Sprint Backlog.
source: Scrum Guide 2020 — Sprint Retrospective (plan improvements).

prompt: Please select which statement is the MOST accurate. Choose the best answer.

options.text: Refinement is a full-time activity during a Sprint for the Scrum Team.
Refinement is a full-time activity during a Sprint between the Product Owner and the Developers.
Refinement is a part-time activity during a Sprint between the Product Owner and the Scrum Master.
Product Backlog refinement is the act of breaking down and further defining Product Backlog items into smaller more precise items.

explanation: Refinement is the ongoing act of breaking down and clarifying Product Backlog items.
source: Scrum Guide 2020 — Product Backlog (refinement).

prompt: Is the Sprint Backlog frozen after the Sprint Planning? Choose the best answer.

options.text: Yes, but only during working hours.
No, the Scrum Master can make changes to it.
Yes.
No.

explanation: The Sprint Backlog is updated throughout the Sprint as more is learned.
source: Scrum Guide 2020 — Sprint Backlog (emerges during the Sprint).

prompt: How much of the Sprint Backlog must be defined during the Sprint Planning? Choose the best answer.

options.text: Just enough tasks for the Scrum Master to be confident in the Scrum Team’s understanding of the Sprint
Just enough to understand design and architectural implications
All of the potential work. The Sprint Planning meeting isn’t over until 100% of the work is identified and estimated
Enough so the Developers can create their best forecast of what they can do, and to start the first days of the Sprint

explanation: Developers plan enough work to forecast and begin; details emerge during the Sprint.
source: Scrum Guide 2020 — Sprint Planning; Sprint Backlog (emergent plan).

prompt: Who can change the Product Backlog? Choose the best two answers.

options.text: The Developers
The Stakeholders, alone.
The Scrum Master.
The Developers but with the permission of the Product Owner.
The Product Owner.

explanation: The Product Owner is accountable for Product Backlog management and may delegate work; changes by others occur under the PO’s authority.
source: Scrum Guide 2020 — Product Backlog management (PO accountable; delegation possible).

prompt: The Sprint Backlog is composed of… Choose the best answer.

options.text: The Product Backlog items selected for this Sprint plus the Team Backlog items.
The Product Backlog items selected for this Sprint.
The plan for delivering Product Backlog items.
The Product Backlog items selected for the Sprint, the plan for delivering them, and the Sprint Goal.

explanation: Sprint Backlog = Sprint Goal (why), selected PBIs (what), and the plan for delivering the Increment (how).
source: Scrum Guide 2020 — Sprint Backlog (composition).

prompt: What happens if a Product Backlog item does not meet the Definition of Done? Choose the best three answers.

options.text: The stakeholders decide what to do with the item.
The Done parts of the item are added to the Increment.
It returns to the Product Backlog.
It cannot be released.
It is not presented at the Sprint Review.

explanation: Work that doesn’t meet the Definition of Done is not part of the Increment; it goes back to the Product Backlog and isn’t shown or released.
source: Scrum Guide 2020 — Definition of Done; Increment (only Done work).

prompt: When many Scrum teams are working on the same product, should all of their increments be integrated every Sprint? Choose the best answer.

options.text: No, that is far too hard.
No, each Scrum team stands alone.
Yes, but only for Scrum teams whose work has dependencies.
Yes, otherwise the Product Owner (and stakeholders) may not be able to accurately inspect what is done.

explanation: A done, integrated Increment must be available at least at the end of each Sprint for effective inspection.
source: Scrum Guide 2020 — Increment (every Sprint results in a Done Increment).

prompt: What is the single source of work undertaken by the Scrum Team? Choose the best answer.

options.text: The Key Stakeholders.
The Project Plan.
The CEO of the organization.
The Product Backlog.

explanation: The Product Backlog is the single source of work undertaken by the Scrum Team.
source: Scrum Guide 2020 — Product Backlog (single source of work).

prompt: When multiple Scrum Teams are working together on a product, what best describes the Definition of Done? Choose the best answer.

options.text: Each Scrum Team uses its own but must make their definition clear to all other Teams so the differences are known.
Each Scrum Team defines and uses its own. The differences are discussed and reconciled during a Hardening Sprint.
It depends.
Multiple Scrum Teams working together on a product must mutually define and comply with the same Definition of Done.

explanation: When multiple teams work on one product, they must share and adhere to a common Definition of Done.
source: Scrum Guide 2020 — Definition of Done (product-level DoD across teams).
